facts.t: The **epidermis** is the outermost skin layer; its layers from deep to superficial are **basal → prickle (squamous) → granular → horny (stratum corneum)**, with a clear layer (lucidum) only on palms and soles.

**Keratinocytes** make up about 90% of epidermal cells and produce keratin; the **stratum corneum** is formed of flat, anucleate keratinized cells (corneocytes). Keratin is the structural protein of skin, hair and nails.
The **basal layer** holds the germinative (stem) keratinocytes that renew the epidermis (turnover about 28 days).

Other epidermal cells: **melanocytes** (pigment), **Langerhans cells** (antigen-presenting; the immune function of the skin) and **Merkel cells** (basal layer; slowly adapting mechanoreceptors for gentle touch and pressure).

**Skin appendages** are hair follicles, sebaceous glands, sweat glands (eccrine and apocrine) and nails; melanocytes, blood vessels and nerves are NOT appendages. The **pilosebaceous unit** (hair follicle + sebaceous gland) is the site of acne.
**Eccrine sweat glands** cover the whole body and control temperature by evaporation; **apocrine glands** are scent glands (axilla, groin).
Skin functions: protection, thermoregulation, sensation, secretion, excretion, immunity and **endocrine** activity (UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into **vitamin D3**).
A full cutaneous examination covers skin, hair, nails and mucous membranes.
**Macule**: flat, non-palpable colour change <1 cm; the same change >1 cm is a **patch** (e.g. vitiligo, pityriasis versicolor).
**Papule**: solid palpable elevation <1 cm (e.g. warts); the classic papular disease is **lichen planus** (flat-topped, polyangular, violaceous, itchy, shiny).
**Plaque**: palpable flat-topped lesion >1 cm with abnormal skin texture, often from coalescing papules, mainly epidermal (e.g. psoriasis).
**Nodule**: solid lesion >1 cm with a deep component in the dermis or subcutis (a dermal lesion, unlike the plaque).
**Wheal**: transient (evanescent) oedematous, erythematous or skin-coloured elevation of variable size from dermal oedema (histamine); the primary lesion of **urticaria**.
**Vesicle** (<0.5 cm) and **bulla** (>0.5 cm) are fluid-filled and differ by size; a **cyst** has a true epithelial wall, whereas a bulla has no wall.
**Burrow**: linear tunnel in the stratum corneum dug by the fertilized female *Sarcoptes scabiei*; the diagnostic lesion of **scabies**. A **furrow** is a deroofed burrow.

A **crust** is a secondary lesion (primary lesions arise first: macule, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle, bulla, pustule, wheal, cyst); it is dried serum, blood or pus (e.g. after herpes simplex vesicles, healing without scar).
**Scales** are laminated masses of keratin from increased proliferation (psoriasis) or decreased desquamation (ichthyosis).
**Erosion** = loss of epidermis only (after rupture of vesicles/bullae), heals without scar; **ulcer** = loss of epidermis and dermis, heals with scar (e.g. ecthyma).
**Lichenification** = thickened skin with accentuated lines from chronic scratching.

**Impetigo** is a superficial infection by *Staphylococcus aureus* and/or group A β-haemolytic streptococci; the lesion is a vesicle/pustule that ruptures to leave a **golden honey-coloured crust** on an erythematous base. Localized disease is treated with a **topical antibiotic** (fusidic acid, mupirocin).
Streptococcal impetigo can lead to **post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis** (not rheumatic fever).

**Bullous impetigo** is staphylococcal: *S. aureus* **exfoliative toxin** splits the upper epidermis, giving flaccid blisters; typical in neonates/infants, spreads by contact, is a superficial infection and heals without scarring.

**Ecthyma** is **ulcerative impetigo**: a deep, streptococcal variant extending into the dermis (vesicle → pustule → thick crust → punched-out ulcer) that heals **with scar** and needs **systemic antibiotics**. Clinical types of impetigo: non-bullous, bullous, ulcerative (ecthyma).
Not bacterial infections: **kerion** (inflammatory tinea capitis) and **acne vulgaris** (a pilosebaceous inflammatory disease, although *C. acnes* contributes).

**Folliculitis** = staphylococcal infection of the upper (superficial) part of the follicle; **furuncle** (boil) = suppurative infection of the lower follicle with a central necrotic core (furunculosis when recurrent).

**Carbuncle** = coalescing deep furuncles draining through multiple openings (a large, indurated, painful plaque, typically on the back of the neck); caused by *S. aureus*, commoner in **diabetic** males and nasal carriers.

**Erysipelas** is a group A streptococcal infection of the **upper dermis and superficial lymphatics**: a sharply demarcated, hot, tender, raised red plaque with fever (deeper involvement = cellulitis); treated with penicillin.
**Lymphoedema** both predisposes to and results from recurrent erysipelas (scarring of lymphatics); it is the commonest complication, with glomerulonephritis also reported.

**Erythrasma** is caused by *Corynebacterium minutissimum*: brown-red scaly patches in intertriginous areas (axillae, groins, submammary), commoner in obese/diabetic patients; treated with erythromycin.
Porphyrins of *C. minutissimum* give **coral-red fluorescence** under **Wood's light** (versicolor fluoresces yellow); Wood's light also helps in diagnosing erythrasma and pityriasis versicolor.

**Leprosy (Hansen's disease)** is caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*, which mainly affects **skin and peripheral nerves**; its target cell is the **Schwann cell**, causing neuropathy and anaesthesia. Typical presentation: hypopigmented lesions with numbness.

The clinical form depends on the patient's **cell-mediated immunity** (not humoral): high immunity → **paucibacillary (tuberculoid)** with few bacilli; poor immunity → **multibacillary (lepromatous)**; borderline forms lie between.
Diagnosis: **slit-skin smear** (modified Ziehl-Neelsen), skin or nerve biopsy (and nasal smears, PCR); the lepromin test is not diagnostic.

**Tuberculoid leprosy** (good immunity, paucibacillary, best prognosis): few well-defined, **hypopigmented, hairless, anaesthetic** patches/plaques; **nerve involvement is early**, asymmetric and severe.

**Lepromatous leprosy** (poor immunity, multibacillary): symmetrical widespread glistening papules, nodules and plaques with thickened nodular ears, diffuse facial infiltration (**leonine facies**) and **loss of the outer third of the eyebrows**.

Lepromatous leprosy also involves **mucous membranes** (nasal infiltration → **epistaxis**, septal destruction), eyes, kidneys, liver, bones and testes; nerve involvement is **late** but extensive (glove-and-stocking anaesthesia of cold areas).

**Dapsone** is the backbone of treatment of all types of leprosy, given daily in **WHO multidrug therapy** with rifampicin ± clofazimine (at least 6 months for paucibacillary, 12 months for multibacillary); retinoids, methotrexate and tetracyclines are not anti-leprotic.

Viral skin diseases: herpes simplex, varicella/zoster, warts (HPV) and molluscum (pox virus); **impetigo is bacterial**. **VZV, HSV and *M. leprae*** are neurotropic, whereas **HPV and pox virus** infect epithelium and are not.
Sexually transmitted skin diseases: **genital herpes, condyloma acuminata and genital molluscum contagiosum**; eczema herpeticum is a complication of HSV, not an STD.

**Herpes simplex** is genital and non-genital (lips, face, fingers, eye), classically at the **mucocutaneous junction**: grouped vesicles on an erythematous base preceded by burning/tingling. HSV stays latent in the sensory (trigeminal/dorsal root) ganglion, so **herpes labialis recurs** (triggers: stress, UV, fever, menstruation); **neuralgia is not a feature**.

**Herpes progenitalis**: grouped painful vesicles/erosions on the genitalia (usually HSV-2, recurrent); active genital herpes at delivery is an indication for **caesarean section** to protect the neonate.
**Herpetic whitlow** = HSV of the finger; HSV can also cause **keratitis** (eye) and encephalitis.
Complications of HSV: **erythema multiforme** (the commonest trigger), eczema herpeticum, corneal ulcers and CNS involvement.
**Tzanck smear** shows multinucleated giant cells in herpes simplex (and in zoster/varicella).

**Chickenpox** is the primary VZV infection (childhood), with vesicles also on the oral mucosa; the virus stays latent in posterior root ganglia and reactivates as **herpes zoster**. Treatment: early antiviral (acyclovir) and vaccine prophylaxis.
**Herpes zoster**: **unilateral, painful grouped vesicles** on an erythematous base along a dermatome; usually not recurrent and gives solid immunity after one attack.
**Post-herpetic neuralgia** (long-standing pain) is the common complication, more frequent in the **elderly**; early antivirals and vaccination reduce the risk.

Zoster is treated with **oral acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days**, started within 48 hours (valacyclovir and famciclovir are alternatives; analgesics/gabapentin for pain); 200 mg five times daily is the herpes simplex dose.
**Warts** are benign epithelial growths caused by **human papillomavirus** (DNA virus, over 200 genotypes), spread by skin contact or fomites; they may involve mucous membranes (e.g. genital warts).

Types: **verruca vulgaris** (hyperkeratotic skin-coloured papules on hands/fingers), **plane warts** (multiple flat-topped papules, often on a child's face) and **plantar warts** (grow inward, tender, painful on walking).
**Condyloma acuminata** (genital warts): soft, pinkish, moist exophytic papules of the genital/perianal skin and mucosa; **HPV 16 and 18** are oncogenic and linked to **cervical cancer**.
Warts are treated by **destruction**: cryotherapy, electrocautery, chemical cautery (salicylic acid), laser; **intralesional steroids and PUVA are not used**. Plantar warts: cryotherapy.

Genital warts: **podophyllin resin 10-25%** (weekly, washed off after 1-4 h), imiquimod, cryotherapy or laser; **podophyllin is contraindicated in pregnancy** and in large bleeding warts (use laser, cryotherapy or electrocautery instead).
**Molluscum contagiosum** is caused by a **pox virus**: firm, **pearly umbilicated papules** from which white cheesy material can be expressed; spread by skin contact (an STD when genital).
Molluscum is treated by curettage, cautery, cryotherapy, laser or chemicals; **steroids are not used**.

**Dermatophytes** are keratin-loving fungi that infect the stratum corneum of glabrous skin, **hair and nails**; sites: tinea capitis (scalp), corporis, cruris, barbae, pedis, manuum and **onychomycosis/tinea unguium** (nail plate: discoloration, thickening, onycholysis).

**Griseofulvin** is the drug of choice for dermatophytes (tinea capitis, corporis, cruris) but is **ineffective against yeasts** (*Candida*, *Malassezia*/versicolor); dose 12.5 mg/kg/day (e.g. 80 kg = 1000 mg = 8 × 125 mg tablets). Terbinafine and azoles are alternatives.

**Scaly tinea capitis**: round scaly bald patch with broken hair stumps and grey scales; **children only** (resolves at puberty), no scarring; fluoresces **yellow-green** under Wood's light (Microsporum).
**Systemic griseofulvin** is the backbone of tinea capitis treatment (6-8 weeks); topical treatment alone cannot cure it because the fungus lies inside the hair.

**Kerion**: inflammatory, boggy, tender, abscess-like swelling studded with follicular pustules (zoophilic fungi), not improved by antibiotics; may cause **cicatricial alopecia** if not treated early.
**Favus**: thick yellow cup-shaped crusts (**scutula**) around hairs, causes **scarring (cicatricial) alopecia**; occurs in children and adults.
**Wood's light** fluorescence: versicolor = **yellow**; erythrasma = **coral red**; favus/scalp ringworm = **yellow-green**.

topics.n: Tinea corporis, cruris, barbae and pedis

facts.t: **Tinea corporis (circinata)**: annular plaque with active scaly/vesicular edge and clearing centre; localized disease → **topical azoles/terbinafine**; extensive or resistant → systemic terbinafine, azoles or griseofulvin.

**Tinea cruris**: scaly erythematous groin patch with active raised border and central clearing, sparing the scrotum; extensive disease → oral terbinafine. Differential: **flexural psoriasis, erythrasma, candidal intertrigo** (not leprosy).
**Tinea barbae**: annular lesion with active border in the beard (farm animals, barber instruments), may be circinate or kerion-like; unresponsive to antibiotics.
**Tinea pedis** (athlete's foot) is common and recurrent; sweating and moisture are predisposing factors.
**Pityriasis versicolor** is caused by the lipophilic yeast ***Malassezia furfur*** (not a dermatophyte); favoured by heat, humidity, oily skin and sweating; recurs in summer.

Clinical picture: asymptomatic hypo-/hyperpigmented (or erythematous) macules with **fine branny scales** on the upper trunk, neck and breasts; more obvious after tanning because the patches do not tan.
Diagnosis: **yellow fluorescence** on Wood's light; KOH shows short thick hyphae with round spores (**"spaghetti and meatballs"**).
Treatment: **topical azoles** or selenium sulfide/ketoconazole shampoo; systemic fluconazole/itraconazole for extensive disease; **griseofulvin and terbinafine do not work**.

*Candida albicans* causes **oral thrush** (whitish pseudomembrane in infants, debilitated adults, HIV; nystatin), **perleche**, intertrigo, interdigital candidiasis (commonly between the **middle and ring fingers**), napkin dermatitis and chronic paronychia. **Favus, kerion and erythrasma are not candidal.**
**Candidal paronychia** (chronic, red swollen nail fold in wet-work occupations) is treated with **fluconazole** and avoidance of moisture.

**Scabies** is a contagious infestation by the fertilized female mite ***Sarcoptes scabiei***; the primary lesion is the **burrow**. Cardinal symptom: intense generalized **nocturnal itching** (worse when warm), often with a family history; lesions are burrows, papules and excoriations, **not scales**.

Adult sites: **finger webs and sides, wrists, elbows, axillae, waist, lower abdomen, genitalia, buttocks and feet**; adults spare the head, neck, palms/soles and **upper back**. Scabies is a cause of pubic itching (with pediculosis pubis).
In **infants** scabies also involves the **face, palms and soles**, with vesicles, pustules, exudation and secondary impetiginization.

**Post-scabietic (nodular) scabies**: intensely itchy nodules, typically on the scrotum/genitalia and axillae, persisting after successful treatment because they are a **hypersensitivity reaction**; treated with **intralesional corticosteroids**.
**Animal scabies**: short incubation, **no burrows**, urticarial, self-limited once the animal is avoided, and **not transmitted human-to-human**.

Scabies treatment: **permethrin 5%** (safe in pregnancy, breast-feeding and infants >2 months; applied to the whole skin and repeated after a week), benzyl benzoate, sulphur, crotamiton or ivermectin; **all family members/close contacts must be treated** even if asymptomatic. Benzoyl peroxide is an acne drug.

**Pediculosis capitis** (*Pediculus humanus capitis*, blood-sucking louse): itchy scalp with excoriations; **nits are eggs firmly cemented to the hair shaft** (unlike dandruff); spread by head contact and by combs, brushes and hats.
Head lice treatment: **permethrin 5%** (repeat after a week because eggs survive), malathion 0.5% lotion, dimethicone or topical ivermectin 0.5%; antifungals and podophyllin are not used.
***Phthirus pubis*** (pubic louse) is spread by close/sexual contact and can infest the **eyelashes** as well as the pubic area.

**Psoriasis** is a chronic immune-mediated (T-cell) papulosquamous disease with genetic susceptibility; **not infectious/contagious**. Basal cell division is accelerated, so **epidermal turnover time is markedly shortened** (normal 28 days). It **improves with sunlight** (flares in winter and in covered areas).

Primary lesion: **red papule covered by loosely adherent silvery-white scales**, coalescing into well-defined, symmetrical plaques with polycyclic outline on **extensor surfaces (elbows, knees)**, scalp and trunk; **psoriasis vulgaris** (vulgaris = common) is the plaque type. Scalp plaques border the hairline sharply and **do not scar** the hair.
**Auspitz sign**: removal of the scales leaves **pinpoint bleeding points** (thin-capped, engorged dermal papillae).

Clinical forms: plaque (vulgaris), guttate, flexural, nail, **erythrodermic**, **pustular (sterile pustules)** and **psoriatic arthritis**; bullous and ulcerative forms do not exist. Nail changes include onycholysis (also seen in lichen planus and onychomycosis).
**Topical** psoriasis treatment: keratolytics (salicylic acid), emollients, corticosteroids, **calcipotriol** (vitamin D analogue), coal tar, anthralin.

**Systemic/physical** treatment for extensive disease: **methotrexate** (dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor), acitretin, cyclosporine, **PUVA/narrow-band UVB** phototherapy; antibiotics such as doxycycline have no role.
**Koebner phenomenon** = new lesions on previously normal skin after trauma; seen in **psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo and plane warts** (not eczema).

**Lichen planus (LP)** is a pruritic immune-mediated disease involving **skin, mucous membranes, hair and nails**; associated with **hepatitis C virus**; not contagious. Types: actinic, annular, atrophic, hypertrophic (no pustular type).

Primary lesion: **pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papule** (flat-topped, violaceous, shiny, fine adherent scales), often on the **wrists and forearms**; **Wickham striae** (fine white reticular lines) on papules and oral mucosa; heals with **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation**.
LP of the scalp destroys follicles → **cicatricial alopecia**; **chronic erosive/ulcerative oral (mucosal) LP and hypertrophic LP are precancerous** (squamous cell carcinoma).
**Actinic LP** (LP tropicus) occurs on sun-exposed skin (**face, dorsum of hands**) and is treated with **antimalarials** (chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine) plus sunscreen.
Treatment of ordinary LP: **topical corticosteroids** for localized disease; **oral corticosteroids** (with sedating antihistamines) for extensive or severe disease.

**Pityriasis rosea** is an acute, self-limited (4-8 weeks), **non-contagious** scaly erythematous papulosquamous eruption, regarded as a viral exanthem related to **HHV-6 and HHV-7**; treatment is **reassurance**, emollients and mild topical steroids/antihistamines for itch.
The **herald patch** (single 2-5 cm oval scaly patch with a collarette of scales, outer erythema) precedes the eruption by 1-2 weeks and mimics **tinea corporis** (KOH distinguishes them).
Secondary eruption: smaller oval scaly lesions on the **trunk and proximal limbs** in a **"Christmas-tree" pattern** along the ribs, sparing face, palms and soles.
Scaly diseases include psoriasis, pityriasis rosea, tinea and seborrhoeic dermatitis; **alopecia areata is non-scaly**.
**DLE** is an autoimmune, **non-contagious**, photosensitive skin disease: well-defined erythematous plaques with **adherent scales**, usually on the face (cheeks, nose), ears and **scalp**.

**Five cardinal signs**: erythema, **telangiectasia**, scaling, **stippling** (dilated pilosebaceous orifices with keratin plugs) and **scarring/atrophy**; pustules and lichenification are not DLE signs.
Scalp DLE ends in permanent **cicatricial alopecia**.

DLE treatment: sun protection, **potent topical (or intralesional) steroids** and **systemic antimalarials** for extensive disease; **PUVA/phototherapy are contraindicated** (lupus is photosensitive).

**Acute eczema** = wet stage: erythema, oedema, papules/vesicles, oozing and crusting; treat weeping lesions with **drying lotions** (potassium permanganate, aluminium acetate), not ointments. **Chronic eczema**: itchy, **lichenified**, excoriated, with pigment change; lichenification is not an acute feature.
**Atopic dermatitis**: hereditary, **IgE-related** (raised IgE; family history of asthma/rhinitis/dermatitis in 50-70%), intensely itchy, irritable infants, non-contagious.

Distribution by age: **infantile** phase (from ~2 months) = weeping papulovesicular eczema of the **cheeks/face**, neck and extensors; **childhood and adult** phases = **flexures (antecubital and popliteal fossae)**, neck sides, with lichenification in adults.
Treatment of flexural atopic dermatitis: **emollients and topical corticosteroids**.
**Seborrheic dermatitis** (associated with *Malassezia* yeast) is treated with oils for infantile scalp crusts, topical antifungals, mild steroids and selenium sulfide shampoo.

**Allergic contact dermatitis** is a **delayed type IV (T-cell) hypersensitivity** in sensitized individuals; the rash occurs at the site of contact (henna, nickel in belt buckles, watch/bracelet band-like rash, footwear on the foot dorsa) and is confirmed by the **patch test**. Irritant dermatitis is non-immunological.
**Urticaria**: sudden itchy **wheals** (transient dermal oedema, heal **without scarring**); acute if <6 weeks; may involve mucous membranes.
Pathogenesis: **type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity**; **mast cell** is the effector cell and **histamine** the main mediator, increasing **capillary permeability**.

**Physical urticaria** (solar, cold, heat, aquagenic, pressure, dermographism) is stimulus-induced; **papular urticaria** (insect-bite hypersensitivity) is not physical and spares mucous membranes. **Cholinergic urticaria**: small wheals after sweating, exertion, heat, hot spicy food or emotion (acetylcholine-stimulated mast cells).

**Angioedema** involves the deep dermis/hypodermis (eyelids, lips) and can be **life-threatening** through **laryngeal oedema**; emergency treatment is **adrenaline 0.5 ml of 1/1000 SC/IM** (300-500 mcg), with IV antihistamines and corticosteroids; salicylates can trigger urticaria/angioedema.
Urticaria treatment: **oral antihistamines are the mainstay**; short courses of corticosteroids (IV in severe cases) are added when needed.

**Drug eruptions** can be exanthematous (papules on erythema, starting proximally, itchy), urticarial, acneiform, eczematous, lichenoid, bullous, pigmented or erythrodermic; **neuralgia is not a cutaneous drug reaction**. **Corticosteroids and anti-epileptics** cause acneiform eruptions (so steroids are not used to treat them).

**Fixed drug eruption** recurs at the **same site** whenever the same drug is taken (lips, genitalia; e.g. sulphonamides, tetracycline), heals with hyperpigmentation; treatment: stop the drug, topical corticosteroid.

**Erythema multiforme**: characteristic **target (iris) lesion** with three concentric zones, often with oral mucosal involvement; the commonest trigger is **herpes simplex**, then drugs, malignancy and pregnancy.

**Vitiligo** is an acquired **depigmenting** disorder caused by **autoimmune (cytotoxic T-cell) destruction of melanocytes**; biopsy shows **complete absence of melanocytes** (in hypopigmentation melanocytes are present but less active). Not contagious.

Primary lesion: well-circumscribed **milky/chalk-white macule or patch** (accentuated under Wood's light), often with white hairs; **asymptomatic** (no itch/pain) - the complaint is cosmetic; can affect the scalp.
Types: **focal, segmental, mucosal** (localized) and **vulgaris (generalized), acrofacial, universal**; there is no papular type.
Generalized vitiligo is associated with other autoimmune diseases: **thyroid disease, alopecia areata**, type 1 diabetes, myasthenia gravis, lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.
Vitiligo may be confused with pityriasis alba, hypopigmented leprosy and pityriasis versicolor.
**Phototherapy** is the backbone of vitiligo treatment (**narrow-band UVB**, excimer, PUVA) because it stimulates residual melanocytes.

Topical options: **corticosteroids** (localized disease) and **calcineurin inhibitors** (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus; especially face and neck); in hepatic failure oral drugs are avoided and topical PUVA, topical steroids or UVB can be used.

**Cicatricial alopecia** = follicles are **destroyed and replaced by scar**, so hair loss is **permanent**; causes: **lichen planus (lichen planopilaris), DLE, favus, kerion**, burns, trauma, zoster; the scalp looks smooth and shiny without follicular openings.
**Non-cicatricial** alopecias (follicle preserved, reversible): **alopecia areata, androgenetic alopecia, telogen and anagen effluvium**.

**Androgenetic alopecia (AGA)**: genetically determined, non-scarring, due to **increased 5-alpha reductase activity** in target follicles (testosterone → DHT miniaturizes follicles). Males: **frontal and bitemporal recession then vertex**; females: diffuse vertex thinning with **preserved frontal hairline**.

AGA treatment: **topical minoxidil** (both sexes), **finasteride** (5-alpha reductase inhibitor, males), spironolactone/antiandrogens (females only), hair transplantation; **corticosteroids have no role**.
**Telogen effluvium**: diffuse, reversible shedding ~3-4 months after a trigger such as **fever (typhoid) or childbirth**, with a normal scalp.
**Anagen effluvium**: toxic injury to actively growing anagen follicles (**cytotoxic chemotherapy**, radiation, heavy metals, methotrexate), causing rapid hair loss soon after starting treatment.

**Alopecia areata** is an **autoimmune**, non-scarring disease against anagen follicles: sudden, asymptomatic, well-circumscribed round patches of hair loss on **normal-looking skin** (no scales); **exclamation-mark hairs** at the margin are characteristic. Associated with thyroid disease, atopy, vitiligo; 10-20% have a family history.
Types: **patchy, ophiasis** (band along the scalp margins; usually **resistant to treatment**), **totalis** (all scalp hair) and **universalis** (all body hair); there is no mucocutaneous type.

Treatment: **topical/intralesional corticosteroids first**, then calcineurin inhibitors, minoxidil, irritants (tincture iodine) and PUVA; **systemic corticosteroids** for resistant or extensive forms (ophiasis, totalis, universalis).

**Acne vulgaris** is a chronic inflammatory (non-infectious, **non-contagious**) disease of the **pilosebaceous unit**, peaking in adolescence (face, chest, back; palms and soles spared). Pathogenesis: androgen-driven **increased sebum**, abnormal follicular keratinization with **keratinocyte proliferation** blocking the orifice, follicular distension and colonization by *Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes*; increased epidermal turnover is not a factor.
Lesions are **polymorphic**: primary lesion = **comedone**, then papules, pustules, nodules and cysts; **vesicles do not occur**. Comedones with few/no papules = mild (non-inflammatory) acne.
**Nodular/nodulocystic** acne causes deep inflammation and therefore **scarring**.

**Retinoids** (vitamin A derivatives) **normalize** follicular keratinization (they do not increase it) and are anti-inflammatory; used **topically** for mild-moderate acne (first-line with comedones/papules) and **orally** for severe disease.
**Benzoyl peroxide** 2.5-10% is a bactericidal topical agent against *C. acnes* without resistance; other topical options: erythromycin/clindamycin and azelaic acid.

**Severe nodulocystic acne** → **oral retinoids (isotretinoin)**, which are **teratogenic** (exclude pregnancy, double contraception); moderate-severe acne may also need systemic antibiotics (tetracyclines, macrolides) or, in hormonal cases, antiandrogens/OCPs.
**Corticosteroids** (topical) worsen or cause acneiform eruptions and **androgens** worsen acne, so neither is used.
